title: UP-024-15 Board Order — Oregon School Employees Association (OSEA) v. North Santiam School District

__________________________________
On June 7, 2016, Administrative Law Judge Martin Kehoe issued a recommended order in
this matter. The parties had 14 days from the date of service in which to file written objections.
See OAR 115-010-0090; OAR 115-035-0050(2). No objections were filed.
When neither party objects to a recommended order, we generally adopt the recommended
order as our final order, and we consider any objections that could have been made to that order
unpreserved and waived. International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local Union No. 659
v. Eugene Water & Electric Board, Case No. UP-008-13, 25 PECBR 901 (2014). Consistent with
that practice, we will adopt the recommended order as our final order in this matter. The final order
is binding on, and has precedential value for, the named parties only. Id. Despite the precedential
limitations of such a final order, we publish the uncontested recommended order as an attachment
to the final order. Clackamas County Peace Officers Association and Atkeson v. City of West Linn,
Case No. UP-014-13, 26 PECBR 1 (2014).
ORDER
1. The Board adopts the recommended order as the final order in this matter.
2
2. The complaint is dismissed.
Dated June 30, 2016.
__________________________________________
Kathryn A. Logan, Chair
__________________________________________
*Jason M. Weyand, Member
__________________________________________
Adam L. Rhynard, Member
*Member Weyand Dissenting
Because neither party filed objections, my colleagues have elected to adopt the
recommended order as final consistent with the approach the Board adopted in International
Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, Local No. 659 v. Eugene Water & Electric Board, Case No.
UP-008-13, 25 PECBR 901 (2014) (EWEB). However, in EWEB, I dissented from the majority’s
decision to utilize this procedure, stating that I would not agree to adopt recommended orders that
I felt incorrectly apply the Public Employee Collective Bargaining Act. I believe this is such a
case. Rather, I would have concluded that there was a change in the status quo and that the
Respondent violated ORS 243.672(1)(e) when it refused to bargain with Complainant before
making the change. Therefore, I respectfully dissent from the order above.
__________________________________________
Jason M. Weyand, Member
This Order may be appealed pursuant to ORS 183.482.

NORTH SANTIAM SCHOOL DISTRICT, ))

A hearing was held before Administrative Law Judge (ALJ) Martin Kehoe on March 7, 2016 in
Salem, Oregon. The record closed on April 15, 2016, upon receipt of the parties’ post-hearing
briefs.
Sarah K. Drescher, Tedesco Law Group, Portland, Oregon, represented the Complainant.
Kelly D. Noor, Garrett Hemann Robertson P.C., Salem, Oregon, represented the Respondent.
__________________________________
On September 9, 2015, the Complainant, the Oregon School Employees Association
(OSEA), filed an unfair labor practice complaint with the Board against the Respondent, the
North Santiam School District (District). That complaint was later amended on
February 26, 2016. The issue currently presented is: (1) Did the District fail to bargain in good
faith with the OSEA in violation of ORS 243.672(1)(e) by refusing to bargain over its decision to
reduce working days and the impacts of that decision, and (2) if so, what is the appropriate
remedy? As set forth below, we conclude that the District did not violate ORS 243.672(1)(e).
4
RULINGS
All rulings of the ALJ were reviewed and are correct.
FINDINGS OF FACT
1. The District is and has been a “public employer” within the meaning of
ORS 243.650(20). It currently manages and provides services for several public schools
including Mari-Linn Elementary School, Stayton Elementary School, Stayton
Intermediate/Middle School, Stayton High School, and Sublimity School. The District’s Food
Service department also provides services for Regis High School, a private Catholic school.
2. Andrew Gardner is the District’s superintendent. Teri Butler serves as the director
of the District’s Human Resources department. Toni Silbernagel is the director of Food Service.
3. The OSEA is and has been a “labor organization” within the meaning of
ORS 243.650(13). It is the exclusive representative of a bargaining unit that includes a variety of
classified District employees. That group includes, in part, a number of employees who work for
Food Service.
4. The OSEA and the District have been parties to a series of collective bargaining
agreements (CBAs). Every one of those CBAs has included a “reopening clause” that allows the
CBA to be modified each spring upon the mutual consent of both the OSEA and the District.
5. The District gives each of its employees a personalized work calendar with a
specific number of workdays prior to the start of every school year. None of the parties’ CBAs
have specified exactly how many days should be included in a given calendar or addressed
reductions in workdays. Moreover, reductions in workdays were not discussed during the
negotiations that led up to the parties’ most recent CBA, which is effective from July 1, 2013
through June 30, 2017.
6. In practice, the total number of days included in any District employee’s work
calendar can vary by position and department and may increase or decrease from one school year
to the next. That is also true for Food Service employees. Nevertheless, when a Food Service
employee is assigned less than 185 days for a particular school year, it is often colloquially
described as a “cut” in workdays.
7. Food Service employees had their work calendars reduced from 185 days in the
2003-2004, 2007-2008, 2008-2009, 2010-2011, 2014-2015, and 2015-2016 school years. The
2003-2004, 2007-2008, 2008-2009, and 2010-2011 reductions were made unilaterally and
without a demand to bargain.
8. To determine how many days work calendars will include each year, the District
typically considers its current and projected finances, costs, and what services are required for
each campus. It also tries to maintain employees’ benefits levels. Occasionally, the District has
asked its employees or the OSEA for input. Food Service employee calendars are ultimately
5
determined by the collaborative efforts of Director Silbernagel, Human Resources, and
Superintendent Gardner.
9. Most Food Service employees work exclusively during the regular school year
and are not required to work during the summer months when school is out. However, any
District employee can choose to complete a special application and compete for extra work
through the District’s summer food program.
10. Most Food Service employees have historically chosen not to participate in the
summer food program, as they often have separate summer jobs or other obligations.
Nevertheless, some Food Service employees have participated in the program in the past.
11. When Food Service employees do apply for the summer food program, they are
given a hiring preference because they would already have the experience necessary to perform
the work. However, if a Food Service employee is ultimately hired for summer work, he or she is
not guaranteed a particular number of hours.
12. In addition to the summer food program, Food Service employees can also take
advantage of other opportunities to work extra hours during the normal school year. Those
include working substitute hours. The District cannot know how many or which substitute hours
will be available in advance of the school year. The number of substitute hours that do become
available fluctuates from year to year.
13. Food Service is partially funded by the federal government and does not receive
funds from the District’s general fund. During the 2013-2014 school year, Food Service was
faced with new federal laws that required that healthier, more expensive foods be served and led
to a significant increase in costs.
14. On May 5, 2014, the District received the results of an audit of Food Service that
had been conducted by an outside, third-party consultant. Among other things, the audit urged
Food Service “to consider a restructuring to reduce the number of the job levels and the number
of managers.” It also suggested that “[t]he district might want to consider assigning some
secretarial time to the food service department to relieve the director from the paper work burden
and allow her to go to schools more often.” (Exh. C-8 at 2.)
15. Negotiations for the parties’ 2014 “reopener” began with a May 14, 2014
bargaining session. In that first session, Superintendent Gardner announced that the District
would be sharing the results of the Food Service audit with the OSEA’s bargaining team during
the next session. Additionally, both parties proposed several unrelated contractual changes.
16. During the second bargaining session, which occurred on May 19, 2014, the
District gave the OSEA a copy of the audit results. Director Butler also announced that the
District would be proposing reducing Food Service employees’ calendar days and having those
employees make up for their lost days by working during the summer months. At that point, Jedd
Rivera, an OSEA field representative, responded that reductions in calendar days could not be
unilaterally implemented and would need to be negotiated. In support of his position, Rivera
6
mentioned the Board’s order in Oregon School Employees Association v. Parkrose School
District, Case No. UP-030-12, 25 PECBR 783 (2013). The District then indicated that it
disagreed with that position.
17. The third bargaining session occurred on May 27, 2014. In that session, the
District shared what it saw as three possible approaches for balancing its budget and
implementing some of the changes recommended by the Food Service audit. After the OSEA
heard those approaches, it indicated that it did not like any of them and said that it would need
more time to review them.
18. Under the District’s first approach, labeled Plan A, four Food Service employees
would have lost ten workdays and three others would have lost two days. The second approach,
Plan B, involved reducing Food Service employees’ benefits and pay. The third approach, Plan
C, would have required Food Service employees to work during the summer.
19. On May 29, 2014, the OSEA took the three plans to its members, who ultimately
voted in favor of Plan A, but also expressed a desire to reduce the number of days that would be
cut. Specifically, they proposed: (1) “The four (4) food service workers that the district proposed
ten (10) days reduction shall only be reduced five (5) days,” and (2) “The three (3) food service
workers that the district proposed to be reduced by two (2) days shall only be reduced by one (1)
day.” (Exh. C-19 at 1.)
20. On June 2, 2014, Rivera sent Superintendent Gardner an email that included a
copy of an arbitrator’s opinion and award (dated May 28, 2013) that resulted from a dispute
between the OSEA and the Sweet Home School District. That same day, the District sent the
OSEA a copy of a letter stating that one bargaining unit employee’s work calendar was being
reduced from 185 days to 180 days.
21. A fourth bargaining session occurred on June 3, 2014. During that session, Rivera
presented the members’ modified version of Plan A. The District then replied that it preferred
Plan C and did not actually want the OSEA to choose a plan. In addition, the District said that it
could simply have implemented any of the plans if it wanted to do so, and indicated that it had
not given up its managerial right to assign workdays.
22. The fifth and final bargaining session for the 2014 reopener occurred on
June 10, 2014. In that session, the District initially attempted to show that Plan C was the
preferable option. However, the OSEA disagreed with that and reiterated that it wanted a
modified version of Plan A. The District then repeated that it could simply choose a plan and that
it was not up to the OSEA to choose. Later, the District proposed its own modified version of
Plan A that included fewer cuts than the District had originally suggested. The OSEA tentatively
agreed to that arrangement.
23. By June 18, 2014, each of the parties had signed a memorandum of understanding
(MOU) memorializing their June 10, 2014 agreement. On June 25, 2014, the OSEA’s members
voted unanimously in favor of ratifying the MOU.
7
24. The MOU specifically provides, “[T]he positions that were originally slated for a
ten (10) day cut, will now be reduced by six (6) work days. Those positions that were slated for a
five (5) day and two (2) day cut will remain at five (5) and (2) day reduction.” (Exh. J-2 at 1.)
The MOU does not overtly address how long that arrangement would remain in effect.
Moreover, prior to signing the MOU, the parties had never discussed that issue.
25. The next round of reopener negotiations (conducted in advance of the 2015-2016
school year) started in early June 2015 and ended around July 17, 2015, when the parties signed
a formal tentative agreement. The subject of reducing Food Service employees’ workdays was
not openly addressed by either party during that reopener period. The parties likewise did not
discuss the MOU signed the year before.
26. On July 21, 2015, the District sent out letters stating that certain Food Service
positions would be cut days. The cuts that were to be made in the 2015-2016 school year were
the same cuts that had been made in the 2014-2015 year. In essence, the District would be
carrying over the terms of the parties’ 2014 MOU.
27. On July 23, 2015, the OSEA sent the District a letter notifying it that the OSEA
desired to negotiate regarding the District’s decision to reduce hours and days in the Food
Service department.
28. On August 3, 2015, the District sent the OSEA a response referencing Articles
4.1, 6.3, and 6.7 of the parties’ 2013-2017 CBA. The response also argued that the District’s
actions were consistent with the parties’ past practice and the status quo.
29. Article 4.1(1)(c) of the 2013-2017 CBA provides, “The District retains the right to
assign, schedule and direct the work of an employee within any given job title in accordance
with the terms of this agreement.” (Exh. J-1 at 7.) Article 6.3 states, “Employees hours per day
shall be assigned at the discretion of the District. The building administrator or director
(whichever is appropriate), shall notify employees of the hours worked per day at the beginning
of the school year.” (Exh. J-1 at 9.) Article 6.7 states, “The District will notify less than
twelve-month (12) employees before the start of their work year as to the number of workdays to
be included in the employee work calendar. Additional workdays may be scheduled as requested
by the building administrator or director (whichever is appropriate), and approved by the
Superintendent.” (Exh. J-1 at 9.)
30. On August 7, 2015, the OSEA sent a new letter to the District stating that the
OSEA desired to negotiate regarding the District’s decision to reduce hours and days in Food
Service as well as the impact of that decision.
31. On August 20, 2015, two of the parties’ representatives met in person and
discussed the District’s planned reduction in hours and workdays. During that meeting, the
District continued to argue that it had a managerial right to reduce employees’ workdays and
accordingly did not need to negotiate that issue. It further suggested that employees who lost
hours could make up for those hours by working substitute hours or working during the summer.
8
32. On August 21, 2015, the District gave the OSEA another response that repeated
the arguments the District made in its August 3, 2015 letter. The response also repeated the
District’s suggestion regarding working during the summer, but added that all Food Service staff
would also have the opportunity to increase the number of workdays via additional work related
to a new YMCA after school program.
CONCLUSIONS OF LAW
1. This Board has jurisdiction over the parties and the subject matter of this dispute.
2. The District did not violate ORS 243.672(1)(e).
Legal Standards
The OSEA’s complaint contends that the District violated ORS 243.672(1)(e), which
prohibits a public employer from refusing to bargain collectively in good faith with the
bargaining representative of its employees. Under the Public Employee Collective Bargaining
Act, the public employer’s duty to bargain is limited to changes to employment conditions that
are deemed “mandatory subjects of bargaining.” For other, “permissive” subjects, the public
employer is free to bargain or not to bargain. However, if a change to a permissive subject has an
impact on a mandatory subject, the public employer may also be required to bargain regarding
that impact. Three Rivers Ed. Assoc. v. Three Rivers Sch. Dist., 254 Or App 570, 574, 294 P3d
547 (2013) (citations omitted).
If the subject in dispute is specifically included in the definition of “employment
relations” under ORS 243.650(7)(a), then the subject is mandatory for bargaining. According to
that subsection, employment relations “includes, but is not limited to, matters concerning direct
or indirect monetary benefits, hours, vacations, sick leave, grievance procedures and other
conditions of employment.” Subjects defined in ORS 243.650(7)(b), (d), (e), (f), and (g) are
permissive. To determine the status of subjects the PECBA does not designate as mandatory or
permissive, we use the balancing test set forth in ORS 243.650(7)(c). Under that test, a subject is
permissive if the impact of the subject on management’s prerogatives is greater than the impact
on employees’ wages, hours, or other conditions of employment. Portland Fire Fighters Assoc.
v. City of Portland, 305 Or 275, 282-85, 751 P2d 770 (1988); Oregon AFSCME Council 75 v.
State of Oregon, Department of Public Safety Standards and Training, Case No. UP-56-99, 19
PECBR 76, 89-92 (2001).
Whenever an unlawful unilateral change is alleged, we first identify the status quo and
determine whether the employer changed it. If the employer did change the status quo, we then
decide whether the change concerns a mandatory bargaining subject. Lebanon Education
Association/OEA v. Lebanon Community School District, Case No. UP-4-06, 22 PECBR 323,
360 (2008). To determine the status quo, we often look to a variety of sources including the
terms of a CBA or other memorialized polices or work rules. In other cases, the status quo can
simply be the product of an employer’s pattern of behavior. See Oregon AFSCME Council 75,
Local 2831 v. Lane County Human Resources Division, Case No. UP-22-04, 20 PECBR 987,
993-95 (2005); Coos Bay Police Officers’ Association v. City of Coos Bay and Coos Bay Police
Department, Case No. UP-61-92, 14 PECBR 229, 233 (1993), citing East County Bargaining
9
Council (David Douglas Education Association) v. David Douglas School District, Case No.
UP-84-86, 9 PECBR 9184, 9192 n 11 (1986).
A past practice is generally characterized by clarity and consistency, repetition over a
long period of time, acceptability to both parties, and mutuality. Lane County Human Resources
Division, 20 PECBR at 993-95. Further, a labor agreement is a type of contract, and
unambiguous contracts must be enforced according to their terms. See Yogman v. Parrott, 325
Or 358, 361, 937 P2d 1019 (1997); Eagle Industries, Inc. v. Thompson, 321 Or 398, 405, 900
P2d 475 (1995); Oregon School Employees Association, Chapter 89 v. Rainier School Dist. No.
13, 311 Or 188, 194, 808 P2d 83 (1991). As a general rule, parties are strictly bound to
agreements they have signed and this Board will not rewrite or reconstitute the language of those
agreements. Gresham Grade School Teachers Association v. Gresham Grade School District No.
4 and Larson, Case No. C-184-78, 5 PECBR 2889, 2895 (1980), remanded for further
proceedings on other matters, 52 Or App 881, 630 P2d 1304 (1981), order on remand, 6 PECBR
4953 (1981).
As the complainant in this contested case, the OSEA bears the burden of proving its
alleged violations by a preponderance of the evidence. ORS 183.450(2); Gallant v. Board of
Medical Examiners, 159 Or App 175, 180, 974 P2d 814 (1999); Ralphs v. OPEU and State of
Oregon, Executive Department, Case No. UP-68-69-91, 15 PECBR 115, 118 (1994). The party
alleging a status quo based on a past practice has the burden of proving its establishment.
Amalgamated Transit Union, Division 757 v. Tri-County Metropolitan District of Oregon, Case
No. UP-62-05, 22 PECBR 911, recons, 23 PECBR 34 (2009); Lane County Human Resources
Division, 20 PECBR at 993.
DISCUSSION
The OSEA asserts, in short, that the applicable past practice and status quo for Food
Service’s classified employees was a 185-day work calendar with a requirement that all
reductions in workdays must be bargained. In our view, that position is largely unsupported by
the evidence presented, which indicates that, historically, the number of calendar days a Food
Service employee is required to work has quite often varied from one year to the next. Although
there is admittedly some evidence of an informal 185-day “baseline” for many Food Service
positions, it is quite clear that that number has never truly been fixed. The record also shows that,
for all of the relevant calendar changes save one, the cuts that the District made were not
negotiated. It follows, therefore, that the practice and status quo identified by the OSEA has not
been “clearly established” as our precedent requires. See Lane County Human Resources
Division, 20 PECBR at 993.
The OSEA contends that the status quo cannot, as the District suggests, be one of
unilateral variability, for that practice has not been sufficiently clear, consistent, or long-lived. In
support of that argument, the OSEA essentially points to the 2014 MOU and the negotiations that
led up to it. On that subject, we would grant that that example shows that the District has not
always made cuts to workdays unilaterally. Nonetheless, one isolated instance does not
necessarily establish a status quo. See Gresham Police Officers Association v. City of Gresham,
Case No. UP-06/18-09, 24 PECBR 55, 71 (2010); McKenzie Education Association/Lane
10
Unified Bargaining Council/OEA v. McKenzie School District 68, Case No. UP-81-94, 16
PECBR 156, 164 (1995). As noted, to be properly established, a practice must ordinarily occur
repetitively over a long period of time. Lane County Human Resources Division, 20 PECBR at
993. Under these circumstances, one could reasonably argue that the parties’ one instance of
bargaining cuts in 2014 is outweighed by the other changes in the record, which include similar
cuts to days, made unilaterally and without complaint, in 2003, 2007, 2008, and 2010.
At the same time, an even more compelling and ultimately dispositive argument can be
made that, if the 2014 MOU is in fact a memorialization of the parties’ negotiated-for status quo
as the OSEA suggests, then the District, by simply maintaining the cuts of that agreement for
another year, has not actually changed anything without bargaining. As the OSEA notes, the
MOU “is devoid of any durational language.” Although either party could argue that it only
meant for the MOU to last one school year, subjective intentions or unspoken understandings
and assumptions do not control. City of Portland v. The District Council of Trade Unions, Case
Nos. UP-58/76-87, 10 PECBR 109, 118 (1987). Put simply, we are not convinced that the plain
text of the MOU is ambiguous. Accordingly, we need not consult extrinsic or parol evidence in
this case, and we will not insert or read in qualifiers – including a duration – that the parties did
not include. See Independent Association of Linn-Benton Community College Classified
Employees v. Linn-Benton Community College, Case No. UP-029-13, 26 PECBR 51, 55-57
(June 2014); AFSCME Local 189 v. City of Portland (Portland Police Bureau), Case No.
UP-49-08, 26 PECBR 62, 638-39 (January 2012).
The OSEA separately argues that the plain language of Articles 4 and 6.7 of the current
CBA does not, as the District argues, give the District the unfettered authority to unilaterally cut
workdays. However, even if the OSEA’s contract interpretation were correct, it would do very
little to establish the past practice or status quo that the OSEA has outlined and thus does not
help the OSEA meet its initial burden. Moreover, we conclude that it is at least equally as true
that the CBA does not expressly state that the District cannot unilaterally change calendars each
year and does not specify precisely how many workdays should be included in them as a default.
In that way, the facts of the instant case can be meaningfully distinguished from those of Oregon
School Employees Association v. Parkrose District, Case No. UP-030-12, 25 PECBR 783,
recons, 25 PECBR 845 (2013), for example, wherein the parties’ contract actually set forth a
negotiated number of workdays for different classified employees. See also Eugene Police
Employees’ Association v. City of Eugene, Case Nos. UP-38/41-08, 23 PECBR 972, 996-97
(2010) (no status quo established by agreements that neither prohibited nor addressed
complained-of action). We further note that a breach of contract, in and of itself, does not violate
